  1. 1

    The function g(x)=−5(x+9)2+4g(x) = -5(x + 9)^2 + 4g(x)=−5(x+9)2+4 is written in vertex form. What is its vertex, and does the graph turn there at a maximum or at a minimum?

    Answer choices for question 1

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Reads hhh straight off the +9+9+9; the template is a(x−h)2+ka(x - h)^2 + ka(x−h)2+k, so x+9x + 9x+9 means h=−9h = -9h=−9.

    You chose C: Takes every vertex to be a minimum, ignoring that a negative leading coefficient turns the parabola over.

    You chose D: Correctly identifies h=−9h = -9h=−9 and k=4k = 4k=4 but reports (k,h)(k, h)(k,h) instead of (h,k)(h, k)(h,k).

    Match the template a(x−h)2+ka(x - h)^2 + ka(x−h)2+k. The inside reads x+9=x−(−9)x + 9 = x - (-9)x+9=x−(−9), so h=−9h = -9h=−9, while the outside gives k=4k = 4k=4 and a=−5a = -5a=−5.

    vertex (−9,4),a=−5<0\text{vertex } (-9, 4), \qquad a = -5 < 0vertex (−9,4),a=−5<0

    A negative leading coefficient opens the parabola downward, so the vertex is the highest point of the graph and 444 is the maximum value.

  2. 2

    Solve (3x+8)(x−6)=0(3x + 8)(x - 6) = 0(3x+8)(x−6)=0.

    Answer choices for question 2

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Solves each factor but keeps the sign the constant is printed with instead of moving it across, giving +83+\tfrac{8}{3}+38​ where −83-\tfrac{8}{3}−38​ belongs.

    You chose C: Reaches 3x=−83x = -83x=−8 and then forgets to divide by the 333.

    You chose D: Divides the coefficient by the constant rather than the constant by the coefficient, giving −38-\tfrac{3}{8}−83​ where −83-\tfrac{8}{3}−38​ belongs.

    The left side is a product of the two real numbers 3x+83x + 83x+8 and x−6x - 6x−6, and it equals zero, so the Zero Product Property forces one of them to be zero.

    3x+8=0 ⇒ x=−83,x−6=0 ⇒ x=63x + 8 = 0 \ \Rightarrow \ x = -\frac{8}{3}, \qquad x - 6 = 0 \ \Rightarrow \ x = 63x+8=0 ⇒ x=−38​,x−6=0 ⇒ x=6

    The solution set is the union of the two linear solution sets, so both values are kept.

    How many real solutions does 4x2+5x+7=04x^2 + 5x + 7 = 04x2+5x+7=0 have?

    Answer choices for question 3

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Adds the 4ac4ac4ac term instead of subtracting it, reading the discriminant as 25+112=13725 + 112 = 13725+112=137.

    You chose B: Reports the axis of symmetry −b2a-\tfrac{b}{2a}−2ab​ as a solution; it is one only when the discriminant is zero.

    You chose C: Treats the discriminant as a hint, when the three cases are biconditionals that settle the count completely.

    Read a=4a = 4a=4, b=5b = 5b=5, c=7c = 7c=7 and compute the discriminant before solving anything.

    Δ=52−4(4)(7)=25−112=−87<0\Delta = 5^2 - 4(4)(7) = 25 - 112 = -87 < 0Δ=52−4(4)(7)=25−112=−87<0

    A negative discriminant puts the vertex clear of the xxx-axis on the side the parabola never returns from, so the curve never meets the axis and there is no real solution. That is a complete answer, not a stalled computation.

  5. 5

    Which of these is x2+14x+5x^2 + 14x + 5x2+14x+5 rewritten in the form (x+p)2+q(x + p)^2 + q(x+p)2+q?

    Answer choices for question 5

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Adds the completing constant 494949 without subtracting it again, so the original constant is left untouched.

    You chose C: Subtracts half of the linear coefficient rather than its square, using 777 where 494949 belongs.

    You chose D: Subtracts the original constant instead of adding it, computing −49−5-49 - 5−49−5.

    Half of 141414 is 777, and 72=497^2 = 4972=49 is the one constant that completes the square. Add it and subtract it in the same line, so the value is untouched.

    x2+14x+5=(x2+14x+49)−49+5=(x+7)2−44x^2 + 14x + 5 = \left(x^2 + 14x + 49\right) - 49 + 5 = (x + 7)^2 - 44x2+14x+5=(x2+14x+49)−49+5=(x+7)2−44

    Expanding (x+7)2−44(x + 7)^2 - 44(x+7)2−44 returns x2+14x+49−44x^2 + 14x + 49 - 44x2+14x+49−44, which is the original expression.

  6. 6

    Solve (x−7)(x+5)<0(x - 7)(x + 5) < 0(x−7)(x+5)<0.

    Answer choices for question 6

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Includes the roots, where the product is exactly zero, though a strict symbol asks for values that are honestly negative.

    You chose B: Keeps the two outside pieces, where an upward parabola is positive rather than negative.

    You chose C: Copies the numbers out of the factors without flipping their signs, so both endpoints come out as the negatives of the roots.

    The product is already compared to zero and already factored, so its roots are x=7x = 7x=7 and x=−5x = -5x=−5, and they cut the number line into three pieces.

    (x−7)(x+5)<0⟺−5<x<7(x - 7)(x + 5) < 0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad -5 < x < 7(x−7)(x+5)<0⟺−5<x<7

    The leading coefficient is positive, so the parabola opens upward and is negative exactly between its roots. The symbol is strict, so the roots themselves are excluded and the interval is open.

    The parabola y=2(x−3)(x+11)y = 2(x - 3)(x + 11)y=2(x−3)(x+11) meets the xxx-axis twice. What is the xxx-coordinate of its vertex?

    Answer choices for question 7

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Reads the zeros as −3-3−3 and 111111, the numbers printed inside the factors, rather than flipping each sign.

    You chose C: Adds the two zeros but never halves, reporting 3+(−11)3 + (-11)3+(−11) as the midpoint.

    You chose D: Names one of the zeros; a zero is the vertex only when the two zeros coincide.

    Factored form displays the zeros: y=0y = 0y=0 at x=3x = 3x=3 and at x=−11x = -11x=−11. Two inputs sharing an output are mirror partners, so the axis of symmetry stands midway between them.

    x=3+(−11)2=−82=−4x = \frac{3 + (-11)}{2} = \frac{-8}{2} = -4x=23+(−11)​=2−8​=−4

    The vertex sits on the axis, so its xxx-coordinate is −4-4−4. The leading coefficient 222 changes how high or low the vertex sits, never where it sits left to right.

    x=−(−7)±(−7)2−4(2)(−5)2(2)=7±49+404=7±894x = \frac{-(-7) \pm \sqrt{(-7)^2 - 4(2)(-5)}}{2(2)} = \frac{7 \pm \sqrt{49 + 40}}{4} = \frac{7 \pm \sqrt{89}}{4}x=2(2)−(−7)±(−7)2−4(2)(−5)​​=47±49+40​​=47±89​​

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    10x2+15x−4x−6=5x(2x+3)−2(2x+3)=(5x−2)(2x+3)=010x^2 + 15x - 4x - 6 = 5x(2x + 3) - 2(2x + 3) = (5x - 2)(2x + 3) = 010x2+15x−4x−6=5x(2x+3)−2(2x+3)=(5x−2)(2x+3)=0

    The Zero Product Property then gives 5x−2=05x - 2 = 05x−2=0 or 2x+3=02x + 3 = 02x+3=0, so the solution set is {−32,25}\left\{-\tfrac{3}{2}, \tfrac{2}{5}\right\}{−23​,52​}, with both elements kept.

    Solve −x2+3x+18≥0-x^2 + 3x + 18 \ge 0−x2+3x+18≥0.

    Answer choices for question 11

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Multiplies through by −1-1−1 and leaves the symbol pointing the same way, which hands back the complement of the solution set.

    You chose B: Excludes the endpoints, though the roots make the quadratic exactly zero and the symbol allows equality.

    You chose D: Takes the endpoints to be the negatives of the roots.

    Make the leading coefficient positive first, remembering that multiplying an inequality by a negative number reverses it.

    −x2+3x+18≥0 ⟺ x2−3x−18≤0 ⟺ (x−6)(x+3)≤0-x^2 + 3x + 18 \ge 0 \ \Longleftrightarrow \ x^2 - 3x - 18 \le 0 \ \Longleftrightarrow \ (x - 6)(x + 3) \le 0−x2+3x+18≥0 ⟺ x2−3x−18≤0 ⟺ (x−6)(x+3)≤0

    The rewritten parabola opens upward, so it is at or below zero on the closed interval between its roots −3-3−3 and 666. Reading the original downward parabola directly agrees: it is at or above zero between those same two roots.

    Three quadratics with integer coefficients: u(x)=x2+9x+5u(x) = x^2 + 9x + 5u(x)=x2+9x+5, v(x)=2x2+9x+9v(x) = 2x^2 + 9x + 9v(x)=2x2+9x+9 and w(x)=x2+9x−5w(x) = x^2 + 9x - 5w(x)=x2+9x−5. Each has two distinct real roots. Which of them factor into linear factors with rational coefficients?

    Answer choices for question 12

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Reads a positive discriminant as a licence to factor over the rationals; it promises real roots and says nothing about which coefficients are allowed.

    You chose C: Computes 4ac4ac4ac as acacac, so vvv gives 81−18=6381 - 18 = 6381−18=63 and every discriminant then misses being a square.

    You chose D: Withholds a verdict the perfect-square test does deliver; these coefficients are rational, which is the one hypothesis that test needs.

    Compute all three discriminants, then ask separately of each whether it is a perfect square.

    Δu=81−20=61,Δv=81−72=9=32,Δw=81+20=101\Delta_u = 81 - 20 = 61, \qquad \Delta_v = 81 - 72 = 9 = 3^2, \qquad \Delta_w = 81 + 20 = 101Δu​=81−20=61,Δv​=81−72=9=32,Δw​=81+20=101

    All three are positive, so all three have two real roots and all three factor over the reals. Only Δv\Delta_vΔv​ is a perfect square, so only vvv has rational roots, and only vvv factors with rational coefficients: v(x)=(2x+3)(x+3)v(x) = (2x + 3)(x + 3)v(x)=(2x+3)(x+3). The other two factor over the reals with irrational coefficients, which is a different claim about a different number system.

    A parabola y=ax2+bx+cy = ax^2 + bx + cy=ax2+bx+c has a<0a < 0a<0 and b2−4ac<0b^2 - 4ac < 0b2−4ac<0. Where does its vertex sit relative to the xxx-axis, and how often does the curve meet that axis?

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Carries over the upward-parabola picture, where a negative discriminant lifts the vertex clear of the axis, without re-reading the sign of aaa in −Δ4a-\tfrac{\Delta}{4a}−4aΔ​.

    You chose B: Reads a negative discriminant as the tangency case; tangency is the case Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0.

    You chose D: Reads a vertex below the axis as forcing two crossings, which holds only when the parabola opens upward.

    Completing the square in general puts the vertex height at −Δ4a-\tfrac{\Delta}{4a}−4aΔ​, so read the two signs one at a time.

    Δ<0  and  a<0⟹−Δ4a=−(negative)(negative)<0\Delta < 0 \ \text{ and } \ a < 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad -\frac{\Delta}{4a} = -\frac{(\text{negative})}{(\text{negative})} < 0Δ<0  and  a<0⟹−4aΔ​=−(negative)(negative)​<0

    So the vertex lies below the xxx-axis. The parabola opens downward, so that vertex is the highest point of the whole curve, and everything else is lower still: the graph never reaches the axis, which is what Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0 says on its own.

    A student tries to solve 6x2−17x+12=06x^2 - 17x + 12 = 06x2−17x+12=0 by hunting for two integers that multiply to 121212 and add to −17-17−17, finds none, and concludes that the equation has no rational solutions. Which response is correct?

    Answer choices for question 19

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Runs the monic pair search on a quadratic whose leading coefficient is 666; the pair has to multiply to ac=72ac = 72ac=72, not to ccc.

    You chose B: Treats the failed search as proving both that real roots exist and that neither is rational.

    You chose C: Turns a failed rational search into a verdict about real roots, which is a different question with a different test.

    When the leading coefficient is not 111, the pair being hunted for multiplies to acacac, not to ccc: here ac=6×12=72ac = 6 \times 12 = 72ac=6×12=72, and −8-8−8 and −9-9−9 do the job.

    6x2−8x−9x+12=2x(3x−4)−3(3x−4)=(3x−4)(2x−3)6x^2 - 8x - 9x + 12 = 2x(3x - 4) - 3(3x - 4) = (3x - 4)(2x - 3)6x2−8x−9x+12=2x(3x−4)−3(3x−4)=(3x−4)(2x−3)

    The formula reaches the same two roots with no search at all, since 289−288=1\sqrt{289 - 288} = 1289−288​=1 gives x=17±112x = \tfrac{17 \pm 1}{12}x=1217±1​, that is 32\tfrac{3}{2}23​ and 43\tfrac{4}{3}34​. A search that comes up empty reports on the list that was searched; here the list was the wrong one.

    The answer

    Part A

    x=−8x = -8x=−8 or x=3x = 3x=3.

    • {−8,3}\{-8, 3\}{−8,3} is the same pair written as a set; reporting only one of the two values is not the same answer, since both satisfy the equation

    Part B

    x=−5+1052x = \dfrac{-5 + \sqrt{105}}{2}x=2−5+105​​ and x=−5−1052x = \dfrac{-5 - \sqrt{105}}{2}x=2−5−105​​.

    • x=−52±1052x = -\tfrac{5}{2} \pm \tfrac{\sqrt{105}}{2}x=−25​±2105​​ is the same pair before the two terms are put over one denominator; a decimal such as 2.622.622.62 is an approximation and not an exact value

    Part C

    The search draws on a finite list of integer pairs, so it succeeds only when the roots are rational. A failed search reports on the list that was searched, not on the equation: the second equation has two perfectly good real roots, and they are irrational, which is exactly what no integer pair could reach.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    The Zero Product Property needs a zero on one side, so move the 242424 across before anything is set equal to zero.

    x2+5x−24=0⟹(x+8)(x−3)=0x^2 + 5x - 24 = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad (x + 8)(x - 3) = 0x2+5x−24=0⟹(x+8)(x−3)=0

    Two numbers multiplying to −24-24−24 and adding to 555 are 888 and −3-3−3. The product is zero, so a factor is zero, giving x=−8x = -8x=−8 or x=3x = 3x=3. Both check in the original: (−8)2+5(−8)=64−40=24(-8)^2 + 5(-8) = 64 - 40 = 24(−8)2+5(−8)=64−40=24, and 32+15=243^2 + 15 = 2432+15=24.

    Part B

    Move the 202020 across and add the square of half the linear coefficient to both sides. Half of 555 is 52\tfrac{5}{2}25​, and (52)2=254\left(\tfrac{5}{2}\right)^2 = \tfrac{25}{4}(25​)2=425​.

    (x+52)2=20+254=1054\left(x + \frac{5}{2}\right)^2 = 20 + \frac{25}{4} = \frac{105}{4}(x+25​)2=20+425​=4105​

    The right side is positive, so take the square root of both sides with both signs, then subtract 52\tfrac{5}{2}25​.

    x=−52±1052=−5±1052x = -\frac{5}{2} \pm \frac{\sqrt{105}}{2} = \frac{-5 \pm \sqrt{105}}{2}x=−25​±2105​​=2−5±105​​

    Nothing in that route can fail, and the quadratic formula returns the same pair, as it must: the formula is this computation carried out once on the general equation.

    Part C

    Factoring over the integers is a search. For a monic x2+bx+cx^2 + bx + cx2+bx+c you look for integers ppp and qqq with p+q=bp + q = bp+q=b and pq=cpq = cpq=c, and only finitely many pairs multiply to ccc, which is why the hunt feels mechanical. It can succeed only when the roots are rational, because an integer pair hands back a factorization with integer coefficients, and that puts each root at a rational number.

    x2+5x−24=(x+8)(x−3),x2+5x−20=(x+52)2−1054x^2 + 5x - 24 = (x + 8)(x - 3), \qquad x^2 + 5x - 20 = \left(x + \frac{5}{2}\right)^2 - \frac{105}{4}x2+5x−24=(x+8)(x−3),x2+5x−20=(x+25​)2−4105​

    For the second, no integer pair multiplies to −20-20−20 and adds to 555, and none ever will, because the roots −5±1052\tfrac{-5 \pm \sqrt{105}}{2}2−5±105​​ are irrational. What follows from the failure is only that the list searched held no answer. The equation still has two real roots, and the route in part B, which guesses nothing, found them.

    So a failed search is a report about the searcher's list, never about the equation, and in particular it is not the claim that there are no real solutions. That is a different claim with its own test, the sign of b2−4acb^2 - 4acb2−4ac, which here is 25+80=105>025 + 80 = 105 > 025+80=105>0.

    In one line

    x2+5x=24x^2 + 5x = 24x2+5x=24 has the roots x=−8x = -8x=−8 and x=3x = 3x=3, while x2+5x=20x^2 + 5x = 20x2+5x=20 has the roots x=−5±1052x = \tfrac{-5 \pm \sqrt{105}}{2}x=2−5±105​​. The integer search finishes the first and can never finish the second, because the roots there are irrational, and that failure is a report about the list of candidate pairs rather than about the equation, which has two real roots throughout.

    Part A

    Take the 555 out of the x2x^2x2 and xxx terms only; the constant carries no xxx and stays outside the bracket.

    5x2+6x−3=5(x2+65x)−35x^2 + 6x - 3 = 5\left(x^2 + \frac{6}{5}x\right) - 35x2+6x−3=5(x2+56​x)−3

    Inside, half of 65\tfrac{6}{5}56​ is 35\tfrac{3}{5}53​ and (35)2=925\left(\tfrac{3}{5}\right)^2 = \tfrac{9}{25}(53​)2=259​, so add that and subtract it in the same line.

    5((x+35)2−925)−3=5(x+35)2−95−3=5(x+35)2−2455\left(\left(x + \frac{3}{5}\right)^2 - \frac{9}{25}\right) - 3 = 5\left(x + \frac{3}{5}\right)^2 - \frac{9}{5} - 3 = 5\left(x + \frac{3}{5}\right)^2 - \frac{24}{5}5((x+53​)2−259​)−3=5(x+53​)2−59​−3=5(x+53​)2−524​

    The −925-\tfrac{9}{25}−259​ is inside the bracket, so the 555 multiplies it too, which is the step the leading coefficient exists to trip.

    Part B

    Isolate the square, divide by the 555 outside it, and take the root of both sides with both signs.

    5(x+35)2=245 ⟹ (x+35)2=2425 ⟹ x=−3±2655\left(x + \frac{3}{5}\right)^2 = \frac{24}{5} \ \Longrightarrow \ \left(x + \frac{3}{5}\right)^2 = \frac{24}{25} \ \Longrightarrow \ x = \frac{-3 \pm 2\sqrt{6}}{5}5(x+53​)2=524​ ⟹ (x+53​)2=2524​ ⟹ x=5−3±26​​

    Now the check, with a=5a = 5a=5, b=6b = 6b=6, c=−3c = -3c=−3. Simplifying the radical and cancelling the factor of 222 common to every term of the fraction gives the same pair.

    x=−6±36+6010=−6±9610=−6±4610=−3±265x = \frac{-6 \pm \sqrt{36 + 60}}{10} = \frac{-6 \pm \sqrt{96}}{10} = \frac{-6 \pm 4\sqrt{6}}{10} = \frac{-3 \pm 2\sqrt{6}}{5}x=10−6±36+60​​=10−6±96​​=10−6±46​​=5−3±26​​

    Part C

    Run the same steps with letters in place of numbers. Dividing by aaa is legal exactly because a≠0a \ne 0a=0, which is the one hypothesis the whole formula carries.

    x2+bax+ca=0⟹x2+bax+b24a2=b24a2−cax^2 + \frac{b}{a}x + \frac{c}{a} = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad x^2 + \frac{b}{a}x + \frac{b^2}{4a^2} = \frac{b^2}{4a^2} - \frac{c}{a}x2+ab​x+ac​=0⟹x2+ab​x+4a2b2​=4a2b2​−ac​

    The left side is now a perfect square by construction, and the right side goes over the common denominator 4a24a^24a2, writing ca=4ac4a2\tfrac{c}{a} = \tfrac{4ac}{4a^2}ac​=4a24ac​.

    (x+b2a)2=b2−4ac4a2\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 = \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}(x+2ab​)2=4a2b2−4ac​

    There is the discriminant, and it was not put there by hand: it is what the right side becomes. Multiplying both sides by 4a24a^24a2 clears the denominator and leaves the square of a whole expression, which is the tidiest place to take a root.

    (2ax+b)2=Δ(2ax + b)^2 = \Delta(2ax+b)2=Δ

    A real square is never negative, so when Δ<0\Delta < 0Δ<0 there is no real solution at all. When Δ≥0\Delta \ge 0Δ≥0 the root comes with both signs, 2ax+b=±Δ2ax + b = \pm\sqrt{\Delta}2ax+b=±Δ​, and dividing by 2a2a2a, which is nonzero, finishes the formula.

    Because every step was carried out on arbitrary aaa, bbb and ccc, the result is proved for every quadratic at once. That is what makes it a theorem: the work in parts A and B was never strictly necessary, because it had already been done in general.

    In one line

    5x2+6x−3=5(x+35)2−2455x^2 + 6x - 3 = 5\left(x + \tfrac{3}{5}\right)^2 - \tfrac{24}{5}5x2+6x−3=5(x+53​)2−524​, so the roots are x=−3±265x = \tfrac{-3 \pm 2\sqrt{6}}{5}x=5−3±26​​, which is exactly what the formula returns. Running the same route on ax2+bx+c=0ax^2 + bx + c = 0ax2+bx+c=0 reaches (x+b2a)2=b2−4ac4a2\left(x + \tfrac{b}{2a}\right)^2 = \tfrac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}(x+2ab​)2=4a2b2−4ac​, so the discriminant is simply what the right side becomes over a common denominator, and the formula is that one computation carried out in general and kept.

    The answer

    Part A

    Δm=169=132\Delta_m = 169 = 13^2Δm​=169=132, so m(x)=(5x−4)(2x+1)m(x) = (5x - 4)(2x + 1)m(x)=(5x−4)(2x+1). Δn=209\Delta_n = 209Δn​=209, which is not a perfect square, so nnn has no factorization with rational coefficients.

    Part B

    A positive discriminant promises two real roots and says nothing about which coefficients are allowed. Over the reals nnn does factor; over the rationals it does not, and no further searching will change that, because 209\sqrt{209}209​ is irrational. The failed search establishes only that no pair on the list tried works.

    Part C

    The test holds for a quadratic whose coefficients are rational: such a quadratic factors over the rationals exactly when its discriminant is a perfect square. The claim is false, and the failure is the hypothesis, since 2\sqrt{2}2​ is not rational. The roots are −2-\sqrt{2}−2​ and −12-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}−2​1​, neither of them rational.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Both have integer coefficients, so the test applies to both. Keep the sign of each negative constant inside the −4ac-4ac−4ac term.

    Δm=(−3)2−4(10)(−4)=9+160=169=132,Δn=9+200=209\Delta_m = (-3)^2 - 4(10)(-4) = 9 + 160 = 169 = 13^2, \qquad \Delta_n = 9 + 200 = 209Δm​=(−3)2−4(10)(−4)=9+160=169=132,Δn​=9+200=209

    A perfect-square discriminant with rational coefficients means rational roots, and each rational root buys a factor with rational coefficients. For mmm the roots are 3±1320\tfrac{3 \pm 13}{20}203±13​, that is 45\tfrac{4}{5}54​ and −12-\tfrac{1}{2}−21​, giving m(x)=(5x−4)(2x+1)m(x) = (5x - 4)(2x + 1)m(x)=(5x−4)(2x+1).

    Now 209209209 lies between 142=19614^2 = 196142=196 and 152=22515^2 = 225152=225, so it is not a perfect square, 209\sqrt{209}209​ is irrational, and nnn has no factorization with rational coefficients. It does factor over the reals, since a positive discriminant gives it two real roots.

    Part B

    Two different properties have been run together. A positive discriminant is exactly the condition for two distinct real roots, and each real root buys a real linear factor, so nnn genuinely does factor over the reals:

    n(x)=10(x−3+20920)(x−3−20920)n(x) = 10\left(x - \frac{3 + \sqrt{209}}{20}\right)\left(x - \frac{3 - \sqrt{209}}{20}\right)n(x)=10(x−203+209​​)(x−203−209​​)

    What the student is looking for is a factorization with rational coefficients, and that demands strictly more. With rational coefficients it happens exactly when the discriminant is a perfect square, and 209209209 is not one, so there is nothing to find and the search would have run out however long it went on.

    What the failed search establishes on its own is only that no pair on the list tried works. A search reports on its own list; the discriminant reports on the quadratic.

    Part C

    The test, with its hypothesis attached: for a quadratic whose coefficients are rational, it factors into linear factors with rational coefficients exactly when its discriminant is a perfect square. Drop the hypothesis and the test says nothing at all.

    The claim drops it. The discriminant really is 111:

So the claim is false, and it is false precisely at the point where the hypothesis was dropped.

    A sum and a product are two numbers, and a pair of roots is two numbers. The parts below pass between the two descriptions and ask what each one settles about the other.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Decide whether two real numbers exist with sum 999 and product 141414, and whether two real numbers exist with sum 999 and product 252525. Give the pair wherever one exists.

      Part B.

      Part C.

    Sum 999 and product 141414: yes, the numbers are 222 and 777. Sum 999 and product 252525: no real pair exists.

    The other root is 555, and k=−3k = -3k=−3.

    A quantity is fixed exactly when swapping the roots leaves it unchanged. r12+r22r_1^2 + r_2^2r12​+r22​ does, equalling (r1+r2)2−2r1r2(r_1 + r_2)^2 - 2r_1r_2(r1​+r2​)2−2r1​r2​, so the coefficients fix it. r1−r2r_1 - r_2r1​−r2​ changes sign, so for two distinct roots only its square Δa2\tfrac{\Delta}{a^2}a2Δ​ is fixed; at Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0 the roots coincide and the difference is 000.

    Part A

The second fails, so no two real numbers add to 999 and multiply to 252525: writing down x2−9x+25x^2 - 9x + 25x2−9x+25 does not conjure them into existence.

    Part B

    The product of the roots is ca=−352\tfrac{c}{a} = -\tfrac{35}{2}ac​=−235​, and one root is known, so divide it out.

    r2=−352÷(−72)=5r_2 = -\frac{35}{2} \div \left(-\frac{7}{2}\right) = 5r2​=−235​÷(−27​)=5

    Now use the other total. The roots sum to −72+5=32-\tfrac{7}{2} + 5 = \tfrac{3}{2}−27​+5=23​, and the sum is −k2-\tfrac{k}{2}−2k​, so k=−3k = -3k=−3.     Part C

    The sum and the product are everything the coefficients report, and both are unchanged when the two roots trade places, because bbb and ccc have no way of telling one root from the other. So a quantity built from both roots is determined by the coefficients exactly when it too survives that swap.

    r12+r22=(r1+r2)2−2r1r2=(−ba)2−2car_1^2 + r_2^2 = (r_1 + r_2)^2 - 2r_1r_2 = \left(-\frac{b}{a}\right)^2 - \frac{2c}{a}r12​+r22​=(r1​+r2​)2−2r1​r2​=(−ab​)2−a2c​

    So the coefficients fix how far apart the roots are and refuse to say which of them lies on the right, whenever there are two of them to tell apart. The one case where the difference itself is determined is Δ=0\Delta = 0Δ=0: the roots coincide, r1−r2=0r_1 - r_2 = 0r1​−r2​=0, and no sign is left to be ambiguous about. 7. A vertex placed to order 14 points

Part A 4

  • Reaches the vertex height as an expression in ccc, from −Δ4a-\tfrac{\Delta}{4a}−4aΔ​ or by evaluating on the axis of symmetry. 2
  • Reads below the axis as a negative height and solves for ccc. 2

Part B 5

  • Turns each root count into the matching condition on the discriminant, or on the vertex height, rather than testing sample values. 2
  • Gets the direction of the inequality right, accounting for the sign with which ccc enters. 2
  • Reports the boundary value separately from the region and says what the curve does there. 1

Part C 5

  • Argues from the vertex being the extreme point of the curve to the number of crossings, rather than quoting the three cases as a rule. 3
  • Says what a negative leading coefficient changes and what it leaves exactly as it was. 2

8. One route run twice, once with numbers and once without 14 points

Part A 4

  • Removes the leading coefficient from the x2x^2x2 and xxx terms only, leaving the constant outside the bracket. 2
  • Distributes the leading coefficient back across both the square and the constant that was subtracted inside it. 2

Part B 5

  • Isolates the square by dividing by the coefficient outside it before any root is taken, and keeps both signs. 2
  • Simplifies the radical and cancels a factor common to every term of the fraction, so the two routes can be compared as written. 2
  • States whether the two routes agree, rather than leaving two unreconciled expressions side by side. 1

Part C 5

  • Carries the same steps through in letters, dividing by the leading coefficient and adding the square of half the new linear coefficient to both sides. 2
  • Shows the discriminant arriving as the right-hand side over a common denominator, and draws the conclusion that the result is proved once for every quadratic rather than remembered. 3

9. Two quadratics one constant apart 15 points

Part A 5

  • Computes both discriminants correctly, keeping the sign of the negative constant term inside −4ac-4ac−4ac. 2
  • Decides each case by whether the discriminant is a perfect square, not by whether it is positive, and names the number system in the verdict. 2
  • Gives a factorization whose expansion returns the quadratic it came from. 1

Part B 5

  • Separates having real roots from factoring over the rationals, and says which of the two a positive discriminant actually delivers. 3
  • States what the failed search does establish, keeping it a claim about the candidates rather than about the quadratic. 2

Part C 5

  • States the test with its condition on the coefficients attached, rather than as a bare equivalence. 3
  • Reaches a verdict on the claim and grounds it in whether the test's hypothesis is met, rather than in the discriminant computation. 2

10. Two numbers named only by their sum and their product 14 points

Part A 4

  • Tests each case against the condition s2−4p≥0s^2 - 4p \ge 0s2−4p≥0 rather than by hunting for numbers. 2
  • Reaches a verdict in each case and produces the pair wherever the condition passes. 2

Part B 5

  • Recovers the second root from one of the two totals rather than by solving the quadratic. 2
  • Uses the other total to pin down kkk, keeping the extra minus sign that the sum carries. 2
  • Checks the pair against both totals, or against a factorization, before reporting. 1

Part C 5

  • Identifies surviving a swap of the two roots as what separates the determined quantities from the undetermined ones. 3
  • Says exactly what the coefficients do fix about the difference, naming its square and connecting that to the discriminant. 2
